sources.title: Christian Clason, Regularization of Inverse Problems (arXiv:2001.00617v2)
sources.locator: Chapter 3 opening and §§3.1–3.2, printed pp. 15–27; Chapter 4 opening and §4.1, printed pp. 30–31.

contents.name: Chapter 3 opening: Hadamard existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence for an operator equation
Example 3.1: differentiating noisy data is unstable in the uniform norm
contents.reason: This is a separate differentiation operator example; IP-01 covers kernel ambiguity, a diagonal Hilbert-space map, and one constrained class.

contents.name: Definition 3.2: least-squares and minimum-norm solutions
contents.reason: The next planned page defines and proves the Hilbert-space Moore–Penrose solution interface; IP-01 does not introduce generalized solutions.

contents.name: Theorem 3.3: the Moore–Penrose inverse on its maximal domain
contents.reason: The planned compact-linear-inverse page owns the domain, range, and minimum-norm properties of the unbounded Hilbert pseudoinverse.

contents.name: Lemma 3.4: Moore–Penrose equations
contents.reason: These operator identities belong with the locally proved pseudoinverse definition and are unnecessary for the metric triangle-inequality lower bound.

contents.name: Theorem 3.5: least-squares and unique minimum-norm solutions
contents.reason: The next planned pair proves the compact linear inverse and Picard range criterion; IP-01 does not claim a generalized-solution theorem.

contents.name: Corollary 3.6: the normal-equation characterization
contents.reason: Normal equations are part of the pseudoinverse development, not a prerequisite for the general indistinguishable-data lower bound.

contents.name: Theorem 3.7: continuity of the Moore–Penrose inverse iff the range is closed
contents.reason: This is a precise operator-specific stability theorem reserved for the next page; IP-01 defines a general class-level modulus without claiming this result.

contents.name: Corollary 3.8: compact operators with infinite-dimensional range have discontinuous pseudoinverse
contents.reason: The result requires compact-operator and range theory; IP-01 instead proves its particular diagonal instability directly.

contents.name: Theorem 3.9: singular-value decomposition for compact Hilbert-space operators
contents.reason: The source theorem is broader than the explicit diagonal witness; the planned next pair supplies the SVD hypotheses and local proof.

contents.name: Theorem 3.10: Picard range condition and pseudoinverse coefficients as stated for y in the range
contents.reason: Clason states this criterion under y in R(K); IP-02 separately requires the orthogonal-complement clause for arbitrary data, so IP-01 does not use the narrower statement as an unrestricted criterion.

contents.name: Section 3.2 discussion: decaying singular values amplify data perturbations and exponential decay gives severe ill-posedness
contents.reason: The general singular-system classification is not proved on IP-01; its single geometric diagonal instance is proved independently in the B-page example.

contents.name: Chapter 4 opening: noisy data and the need to approximate a discontinuous inverse
Definition 4.1: a regularization as continuous operators approximating the pseudoinverse
contents.reason: IP-01 separates estimator stability from regularization but defines no regularization family or parameter choice procedure.

contents.name: Theorem 4.2: a regularization of a discontinuous inverse cannot be uniformly bounded
contents.reason: The Banach–Steinhaus regularization result is outside this page's triangle-inequality lower-bound scope and belongs with parameter-choice analysis.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3: divergence off the pseudoinverse domain under a uniform forward-operator bound
contents.reason: This result assumes a regularization family and a uniform operator bound, neither of which is part of the IP-01 model or proof.

contents.name: Definition 4.4: a priori, a posteriori, and heuristic parameter-choice rules
contents.reason: Parameter-choice taxonomy has a dedicated planned page and is deliberately not conflated with identifiability or stability here.

sources.title: Tristan van Leeuwen and Christoph Brune, 10 Lectures on Inverse Problems and Imaging, version 1

contents.name: Section 1.2: the forward-operator equation, parameter/data spaces, and solution set
Section 1.2: Hadamard existence, uniqueness, stability, and additive-noise model
Section 1.3.1: scalar rootfinding sensitivity when the derivative is small
contents.reason: This local nonlinear example is not one of IP-01's three assigned B leaves and is not needed for the general metric theorem.

contents.name: Section 1.3.2: finite-dimensional matrix inversion and condition-number error amplification
contents.reason: This finite matrix condition-number estimate is distinct from the infinite diagonal discontinuous-inverse witness authored for IP-01.

contents.name: Section 1.3.3: differentiation with uniformly small data error and fixed reconstruction error
contents.reason: This second differentiation illustration is a separate operator example; the assigned leaves already cover a kernel, a diagonal map, and a constraint.

sources.title: Giannis Daras et al., A Survey on Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems (arXiv:2410.00083v1)

contents.name: Section 1.2: information loss makes the recovery target important to specify
contents.reason: The survey's sweeping qualitative claim is not used as a theorem supplier; IP-01 proves only the stated pairwise ambiguity and stability bounds.

contents.name: Section 1.2: MAP, MMSE, and posterior sampling are distinct recovery targets
contents.reason: These statistical recovery targets are outside this deterministic metric-space page and have separate planned Bayesian prerequisites.

contents.name: Section 1.2 report of the perception-distortion theorem by Blau and Michaeli
contents.reason: The survey cites this result but its underlying theorem was not independently read and is not needed for the local triangle-inequality proof.
